specAnchors.text: explain the trend in reactivity in Group 7 in terms of electronic configurations

primer.text: From Group 7 (Halogens) you already know that each halogen carries seven electrons in its outer shell and commonly forms a 1- ion. This note explains why reactivity falls down the group: gaining that extra electron becomes harder the further the outer shell sits from the nucleus, which is the exact opposite of the Group 1 pattern.

modules.title: Group 7: Reactivity & Electronic Configurations
modules.opening: When halogen atoms react they gain one electron to complete their outer shell, forming negative ions called halide ions. This gain is what makes them reactive, and how easily it happens decides the reactivity order. Down the group the growing number of shells pushes the outer shell further from the nucleus, so the reactivity of the halogens decreases.
keyPoints: Halogen atoms gain one electron during reactions to form -1 ions called halide ions.
Reactivity of the Group 7 non-metals decreases as you go down the group.
The number of electron shells increases by one with each element down the group.
The growing distance from the outer shell to the nucleus makes the halogens less reactive.
Fluorine, with the smallest atom, is the most reactive halogen in the group.

low.restatement: Halogens react by gaining one electron into their outer shell, and the ease of that gain falls down the group. More shells mean the incoming electron is further from the nucleus and less strongly pulled in.
low.analogy: Like trying to signal a friend across a growing crowd: the further they stand back, the weaker the pull of your wave.
low.examPointer: State the trend, then give the electron-gain reason; examiners award the mark for the configuration-based explanation.

medium.restatement: Each halogen needs exactly one electron to complete its outer shell, so reactivity measures how strongly the atom attracts that electron. Added shells down the group increase the distance between nucleus and outer shell, weakening the attraction and lowering the reactivity from fluorine to iodine.
medium.analogy: Picture a magnet drawing in a stray pin: slide extra sheets of paper between them and the pin settles onto the table more and more easily unclaimed.
medium.examPointer: Answers earn full credit by linking distance, attraction and ease of electron gain in one chain, not by quoting the trend alone.

modules.title: Electronic configuration of Group 7 elements
modules.opening: The atoms of every Group 7 element show seven electrons in their outer shell, one short of a complete set. As you descend the group, one extra filled shell is added at each element, so the outer shell sits progressively further from the nucleus. The forces of attraction for the incoming electron therefore weaken, making each halogen below the last less able to gain its electron and so less reactive.
keyPoints: All Group 7 atoms have seven electrons in their outermost shell.
Descending the group adds one filled shell at each element.
The added shells carry the outermost shell further from the nucleus.
The attraction between the nucleus and the incoming electron grows weaker with distance.
Gaining the electron becomes harder down the group, so reactivity falls.

low.restatement: Every halogen is one electron short of a full outer shell. Down the group the extra shells push that shell outward, the nucleus holds the incoming electron less tightly, and reactivity drops.
low.analogy: Catching a ball thrown from further and further away gets harder each time; the electron faces the same fading reach.
low.examPointer: Shell diagrams of the halogens often appear in questions; use them to read off the seven outer electrons and the growing distance.

medium.restatement: The fixed seven-outer-electron pattern means the trend comes entirely from distance: each element down the group adds a complete inner shell, increasing the radius of the outermost shell. Electrostatic attraction for the electron to be gained weakens with that distance, so fluorine reacts fiercely and iodine sluggishly.
medium.analogy: Think of gravity weakening with orbital distance: a far satellite drifts free with the slightest tug, just as a distant outer shell barely pulls the electron in.
medium.examPointer: Compare with Group 1 in your answer when asked: one group loses electrons, the other gains them, and their trends run in opposite directions.

glossary.definition: The -1 ion formed when a halogen atom gains one electron to complete its outer shell.
The arrangement of electrons among the shells of an atom.
The positively charged centre of an atom, which attracts the outer electrons.
The pull between opposite charges, here between the positive nucleus and the negative electrons.
A measure of how readily an element takes part in chemical reactions.

workedExample.prompt: a) State the reactivity trend down Group 7 and explain it in terms of electronic configurations. b) Why is fluorine the most reactive halogen? c) How many electrons does each Group 7 atom hold in its outer shell, and what ion forms when a halogen reacts?
steps: a) Reactivity decreases down the group: each element adds one filled shell, so the outer shell — and the electron to be gained — sits further from the nucleus.
The greater distance weakens the attraction of the nucleus for the incoming electron, so gaining it becomes harder and reactivity falls.
b) Fluorine is the smallest halogen, so its outermost shell is closest to the positive nucleus and its pull on an extra electron is the strongest of the group.
c) Every Group 7 atom has 7 outer electrons; gaining one more forms a negative halide ion with a 1- charge.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Less reactive down the group — more shells, greater distance, weaker attraction for the gained electron. b) Smallest atom, strongest attraction. c) 7 outer electrons; a 1- halide ion forms.
